name: Bishop and knight endgames
goal: You can tell when a bishop beats a knight and when the reverse is true, and know two draws: bishops of opposite colours, and the wrong bishop with a rook pawn.

intro.text: When only bishops, knights and pawns are left, the kind of piece you have can matter as much as the number of pawns. A bishop is at its best on an open board with pawns on both sides, because it works from far away; a knight is better when the pawns are locked and the enemy pawns sit on the bishop's colour. And some of these endgames are drawn even a pawn down: bishops of opposite colours often draw, and so does a rook pawn whose bishop cannot control the queening square.

parts.title: The long-range bishop
parts.keyIdea: On an open board a bishop can watch both sides at once from far away, while a knight needs several jumps to switch sides.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White, the pawns are level and there are pawns on both sides of the board. Your pawn on a5 is passed, and Black's knight on d4 would like to jump across to stop it. Find a bishop move that keeps the knight away.

credit.authors: Lichess; the players of the game

notes.text: From d7 the bishop covers b5, c6 and e6, the squares the knight would use to come near your pawn. The bishop does this from far away, while the knight would need several jumps to get round.
Black's king attacks your bishop, but ignore it and push. If the king takes on d7, it is too far from the a-file, and the knight still cannot reach a square in front of the pawn in time.
The pawn queens next move and nothing can stop it. Your bishop was worth giving up: it kept the knight away just long enough.

parts.title: The knight against a bad bishop
parts.keyIdea: When the pawns are fixed on the bishop's colour, the bishop has nothing to attack, and a knight can settle on a square no pawn can reach.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White. Every Black pawn stands on a light square, the same colour as Black's bishop, and most of the pawns are locked against each other. Your knight on d1 is far from the action: find it a better home.

credit.authors: Lichess; the players of the game

notes.text: The knight sets off for c5. It cannot get there in one jump from d1, so it goes round by b2 and d3. On c5 no black pawn will ever be able to attack it, because Black's b- and d-pawns have already gone past.
One more step. From d3 the knight can jump to c5 or e5, and Black's bishop can never cover either square, because both are dark.
The knight lands on c5 and attacks the pawns on a6 and e6. Nothing defends the pawn on a6, and Black's bishop is stuck behind its own pawns with nothing to attack.

parts.title: Bishops of opposite colours
parts.keyIdea: With bishops of opposite colours, stop the enemy pawn on a square of your bishop's colour: the other bishop can never attack that square.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You are White and a pawn down. Your bishop moves on light squares and Black's on dark ones. Black's pawn on c3 is only two steps from queening.

credit.authors: Lichess; the players of the game

notes.text: Your bishop guards c2, the next square on the pawn's path. That square is light, so Black's bishop can never attack your bishop there or help the pawn forward. It is the only move that holds: anything slower lets the pawn queen.
Black's bishop now attacks your pawn on f2. Your king steps to f1, still guarding the pawn, and starts walking towards the c-pawn.
The king still guards f2 and comes closer to the c-pawn. With the pawn stuck on c3, Black's extra pawn is not enough, and the Engine judges the position a draw.

parts.title: The wrong bishop
parts.keyIdea: A rook pawn whose bishop cannot control the queening square is a draw once the defending king reaches the corner.
parts.text: From a game played on Lichess. You only have your king left. Black has a bishop and a pawn on the a-file, but the bishop moves on light squares, and the pawn would queen on a1, a dark square. Can your king get to that corner in time?

credit.authors: Lichess; the players of the game

notes.text: Head for the corner. From d3 the king reaches c2 next, and Black's king and bishop cannot keep it out of the corner from there. Every other move here loses.
Keep going. Your king is now two steps from a1.
The only move that holds, because Black's king now controls b2. Once your king is in the corner, Black cannot drive it out: a1 is a dark square, so the bishop can never attack it.
